title: Static binary releases
body:
## The issue

tmux is an integral part of my dev workflow which means I take it with me everywhere. I use it on any machine I'm on, any server I ssh onto and even inside docker containers.

The servers I'm working on usually only come with an out-of-date version of tmux which are incompatible with my tmux.conf.

Now your install guide offers various options on how to get a current version but it does not talk about statically linked binaries. I found that using those is by far the easiest method for deploying tmux on basically any system (especially without sudo permissios). There is a project out there providing these binaries (at least for x86 and arm64 architectures) which are built in the GitHub CI: https://github.com/pythops/tmux-linux-binary.

Instead of just downloading the binary manually, I use a tool called [mise-en-place](http://github.com/jdx/mise/) to download and update it in a more automated fashion.

## Improvement ideas

For me personally, the distribution could be improved in one of the following ways (ordered by increasing amount of work but also more "official" release channel):
- Link above repo in the install section of the readme. That keeps things as is but at least people are aware of this option making it less likely for the repo to die.
- Fork/copy above repo into the tmux namespace. That keeps things separate still but the release feels more official/legit. That might allow integrating it e.g. into the package registry of mise-en-place.
- Attach the pre-built binaries to the releases of this (the main) repository. That would of course require either an updated release workflow or you to manually attach the assets to the GitHub release.

---

I am willing to contribute here via a PR or even by maintaining a release repository in the tmux namespace but I want to get your take on this before investing any effort in either one of these options.

P.S.: I saw the issues regarding Appimage releases. Those don't work for me as they don't go so well with docker containers and caused a few other annoyances.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: The tricky bit will be ncurses because if you link tmux against ncurses 6 you may not be able to use it on platforms where the compiled terminfo db is from ncurses 5 and vice versa. I don't know if it is possible to compile the entire terminfo db into ncurses, there is  `--with-fallbacks` but then you are limiting the available terminfo entries.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
ncurses6 can "always" read ncurses5 terminal databases.
Applications built with ncurses5 can't read numbers larger than 32767 (e.g. `pairs`)
Compiling the entire database as fallbacks might be doable, but a lot of work.
That's an [FAQ](https://invisible-island.net/ncurses/ncurses.faq.html#big_terminfo), anyway.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
So I got started and [this Dockerfile](https://github.com/reporter/tmux-releases/blob/183b411d9f534e197dea0838d4c1cec97e7feb74/Dockerfile) is more or less what I had in mind. I will automate the build for different architectures using the GitHub CI and I still have to look into what's the best strategy for macOS (and maybe FreeBSD targets).

I will compile against ncurses6 but the build recipe is configurable. The releases would then target ncurses6. The 6.0 release is a decade old so I reckon not a lot of people will run into that issue. And if they do, the can run a build themselves using ncurses5 via a build arg.

Does that make sense?

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: I think that is fine especially if ncurses 6 can read ncurses 5 compiled dbs.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
It was more painful than I care to admit but I now created a GitHub workflow that will create static binaries for Linux and macOS, x86 and arm64 each. See the [release I created for 3.6a](https://github.com/reporter/tmux-releases/releases/tag/v3.6a).
It is also possible to build the binaries locally using either the build scripts or more conveniently the docker setup.

I tested the Linux x86 version locally. For all other builds I only run a very basic sanity check in the CI confirming the builds are in fact static (or at least as static as it gets for macOS) and are able to start, list and kill a session.
If someone with some apple hardware is willing to actually try the binary, I'd very much appreciate that.

@participant1 would you mind to take a look at the build scripts [in the scripts directory](https://github.com/reporter/tmux-releases/tree/main/scripts) to sanity check the configure options I used?

I think the missing platforms are armv7 for Linux and FreeBSD. I would integrate those in a future PR as I'm a little fed up with GitHub workflows right now and I assume they will be a little trickier since afaik GitHub doesn't offer native runners.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: The scripts look OK to me. It might be worth building tmux with `--with-TERM=screen-256color` or `screen` because some older platforms will not have `tmux` or `tmux-256color`.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Actually it turns out that checksums are a builtin feature of GitHub nowadays. See [here](https://github.blog/changelog/2025-06-03-releases-now-expose-digests-for-release-assets/) for reference. When you click the release page, the checksum are listed next to each artifact and also accessible via the REST API.

So where do we go from here? I'd love to have that repo fly under the "official" tmux flag, i.e. in the tmux namespace. Is that still an option for you? Is there something missing that would need to be added before? As I mentioned before, I'd be happy to maintain it and make sure it stays up to date with the tarball releases.
For my personal use the current setup works as well though, so if you just want to link to it in the wiki that would also work.

I'm sure that would be possible but definitely requires some changes to the current setup. E.g. I'm not sure how the tagging would work (afaik a release requires a corresponding tag) for a nightly build. But there are repos out there doing it, so it's got to be possible. I'll look into that.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
I would probably take the LICENCE or COPYING file from each dependency tarball (the one actually used for the tmux build so best if this can be done by the scripts not manually) and either put them together in a file LICENCES.tar.gz as `LICENCE.libevent`, `COPYING.ncurses` etc, or add them each to the release separately (one tarball would be better if possible). I would also include tmux's own LICENCE file. I'm not sure it is required for ncurses and musl but it can't hurt. libevent's is pretty clear:
~~~~
2. Redistributions in binary form must reproduce the above copyright
   notice, this list of conditions and the following disclaimer in the
   documentation and/or other materials provided with the distribution.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: musl is mostly 2 clause BSD but it has at least one file under 3 clause BSD which has the same language as libevent above.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
utempter is unfortunately LGPL and among the reams of verbiage is this text which requires the same:
~~~~
  6. As an exception to the Sections above, you may also combine or
link a "work that uses the Library" with the Library to produce a
work containing portions of the Library
...
You must give prominent notice with each copy of the work that the
Library is used in it and that the Library and its use are covered by
this License.  You must supply a copy of this License. 
~~~~
There is also some guff about a "written offer" to provide the source code on request, but I'd say including the licence itself is sufficient to imply that, there is no point in going crazy.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Ok, the licenses shouldn't be too big of a deal. Adding them all to one archive should be simple enough so I don't see a reason not to do that.

Neovim releases nightly using a [GitHub workflow](https://github.com/neovim/neovim/blob/master/.github/workflows/release.yml). I'll find some inspiration in there and am pretty positive that I can make it work.

There are some [docs on transferring a repo](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/creating-and-managing-repositories/transferring-a-repository). There is one paragraph that sounds a little scary:

> If the transferred repository contains an action listed on GitHub Marketplace, or had more than 100 clones or more than 100 uses of GitHub Actions in the week prior to the transfer, GitHub permanently retires the owner name and repository name combination (OWNER/REPOSITORY-NAME) when you transfer the repository. If you try to create a repository using a retired owner name and repository name combination, you will see the error: "The repository REPOSITORY_NAME has been retired and cannot be reused."

I didn't count the number of workflow runs so far and I doubt they are near 100 but each of them contains several actions. I have no idea how that is counted.
I suppose using that repo transfer is especially important if you want to keep everything surrounding the code (issues, PRs, stars, forks, etc.). But since the repo doesn't have any of those right now, I'd suggest you just create an empty repo and give me permissions for it. I will then just archive the repo in my namespace and push my local repo to the new origin. For our use case, I'd image that is sufficient.

I will be busy with a couple of other things in the next few days, so I'm not sure I can get the nightly releases to work before Christmas. Maybe I'll just ping you when I'm done with all that and we move the project then?

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: Yes that's fine, there is no rush, thanks. Nightly releases is probably not warranted unless you can make it only release if something changed since the last release, weekly would be enough.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Alright @participant1 , I did get around to work on this on the weekend. The workflow now contains some significant changes and is in a pretty good state right now I think. The most notable changes:
- The binaries are now compressed (as suggested by you earlier)
- All license files are collected in a separate job and added to each releases as a single archive
- The workflow now runs once a day to produce binaries built of the current master branch (I called these preview builds). If no changes have been made to the tmux repo, the build is skipped and no new release is created. If there have been changes, the binaries are built and published as a new pre-release. Build artifacts are kept for 90 days, so it is possible to download older builds if that's necessary for whatever reason.
- The workflow definition obviously got a little more complex in the course of all this but I did try to refactor it in a way to keep it as simple/clean as possible for ease of maintenance. 
- The readme now describes both how to install from a release and how to build locally.

Take a look at [the release](https://github.com/reporter/tmux-releases/releases) page for reference.

Anything I missed?

I don't think there is a real downside to doing so, it might even be a little more future proof in case we ever want to ship additional files like a readme or something.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Just a quick follow-up, in case this is interesting for anyone else:

I managed to get the new build repo merged into the tool registry of mise-en-place. That means tmux can be installed using `mise use --global tmux`. Updating is then handled via `mise update`.

I like managing my dev tooling this way, since it's super portable and does not require sudo permissions.
